title: The date is hard to read
script: Hi, I've looked at the poster on my phone. The café name is clear, but I can barely read the opening date. Could you make that easier to see? I'd like to keep the warm colors and the gold line. Thanks. Send me a quick preview before you export the final file.

gist.question: What is the client mainly asking for?

details.question: Where did the client view the poster?
What should remain?
choices: The warm colors and gold line.

phrases: I can read it only with difficulty.
The client wants a preview before the final files.
response: Respond to the readability problem, preserve what the client likes, and confirm the proof.
model: I’ll make the opening date easier to read while keeping the warm palette and gold line. I’ll send a phone-size preview before exporting the final file.

title: “Make it pop” with a clue
script: Thanks for sending the draft. It feels close to our style, so I don't want to start again. Could you make the offer pop a little more? The fifty percent discount is the reason we're posting this. Please keep the logo where it is, and show me two options for the offer rather than changing the whole design.

gist.question: What does “make it pop” mean here?

details.question: What must stay in its position?
How many offer options does the client want?

phrases: Begin the design from the beginning.
Choose one action instead of another.
response: Clarify or confirm the requested emphasis and propose the two options.
model: I’ll keep the logo and overall style, then show two ways to emphasise the fifty percent offer. Would you prefer a size change in one version and a stronger color contrast in the other?

title: A second language version
script: Hello, the English poster is approved. We also need a version in Arabic for the campaign. I've got the approved translation, and my colleague can check the proof. I know we've used the two revision rounds already. Please send me the extra fee and the new delivery date before you begin. The brand mark should stay exactly as it is.

gist.question: What new work does the client need?

details.question: Who can review the proof?
What must happen before work begins?
choices: Confirm the extra fee and delivery date.

phrases: The client has confirmed the exact translated wording.
Agree on the additional work and terms first.
response: Confirm the new deliverable, the reviewer, what stays unchanged, and the quote.
model: I’ll quote for the Arabic version and confirm the new delivery date before starting. I’ll use the approved translation, keep the mark intact, and send a proof for your colleague’s review.

title: A deadline with a missing detail
script: Hi, just checking on the first draft. Our team meeting is tomorrow afternoon, and I'd like something we can discuss there. It doesn't have to be the final version yet. Please tell me what is ready, what you still need from us, and when you'll send the preview. We're working in different time zones, so please include the time zone in your message.

gist.question: What does the client need before the meeting?
choices: A discussion preview and clear status.
No update until after the meeting.

details.question: Does the preview need to be final?
choices: No. A discussion draft is enough.
Yes. All files must be final.
The client does not mention the issue.

details.question: What must the delivery time include?

phrases: A draft good enough for a team conversation.
response: Give an honest progress update. If you do not know the meeting time, ask rather than invent a deadline.
model: The layout is ready for discussion, but I still need the approved prices. What time is your meeting, and which time zone are you using? I’ll confirm when I can send the preview once we agree that timing.

title: A tone for the audience
script: I've compared the two mood boards. The bright version is fun, but our daytime customers mostly come to read and have quiet conversations. I prefer the softer version for this poster. We can use a more energetic style for evening events later. For now, keep the invitation calm and make the practical details easy to find.

gist.question: Which direction fits this poster?
choices: A style chosen without considering the audience.

details.question: Who is this version for?
choices: Daytime customers who read and talk quietly.

details.question: When might an energetic version be useful?

phrases: This is the current decision, not a permanent rule.
The information viewers need to act.
response: Recommend the current mood and distinguish it from the later campaign.
model: I’ll use the softer version for the daytime invitation and keep the practical details clear. We can develop an energetic version for evening events later. Could you confirm the opening time and location?

title: The file we need to edit
script: The image looks good, but our staff need to change the price each week. Right now, all the words seem to be part of the picture. Could you send an editable version with the price in its own text layer? We use Canva here. A normal image preview would still be useful, but it won't replace the working file.

gist.question: What is the main unmet requirement?
choices: Editable price text in the working file.

details.question: Which editor does the team use?
What does the client say about the normal image preview?
choices: It is useful but does not replace the working file.
It is the only file needed.

phrases: The price must be separately editable.
The preview is not a substitute for the source.
response: Confirm the compatible source file and the separate preview.
model: I’ll prepare a Canva source with the price in a separate editable text layer and include a normal image preview. Could someone on your team test the price edit before I finalise the delivery?

title: Nike: simplicity and interpretation
script: Look at the Nike mark without the word. It is one curved shape, with a broader section at one end and a narrower tip at the other. The mark has very little internal detail, so we can still see its outline when it becomes small. To me, the curve suggests movement. That is an interpretation, rather than a fact the shape proves. In an analysis, describe the visible shape first, then explain what it may suggest and how it works at a smaller size.

gist.question: What does this analysis connect?
choices: A simple shape, small-size use, and a possible reading.
A comparison of two typefaces in the wordmark.
A recommendation to add more internal detail.

details.question: Which observation is visible?
choices: The outline has very little internal detail.
The outline contains several separate small shapes.
The main feature is a textured surface.

details.question: How is “movement” presented?
choices: As the documented intention of the original designer.
As the only reading the audience can have.

phrases: The speaker qualifies a personal interpretation.
response: Analyse the mark in three sentences: visible fact, possible reading, practical test.
model: I notice a single curved shape with little internal detail. To me, it suggests movement. I would test its outline at a small size before making a similar design choice for a new client.

title: Microsoft: shape, space, and repetition
script: The Microsoft symbol uses four colored squares. They sit in a two-by-two arrangement, with clear gaps between them. The repeated square shape and the regular spacing make the group feel organised to me. Notice that repetition does not require one color: the shape repeats while the colors differ. We can describe those choices without claiming that each color has one universal meaning. When analysing a new mark, ask which features repeat, which features change, and what remains recognisable when the mark is small.

gist.question: What repeats in this symbol?
choices: The square shape and regular arrangement.
A single color across every part.
A shading effect that makes the squares look three-dimensional.

details.question: How many squares are there?
What differs between the squares?
choices: The colors differ while the square shape repeats.
The shapes differ while every color stays the same.
The gaps disappear as the colors change.

phrases: One feature changes while another stays consistent.
response: Describe two elements and one principle, then give a small-size test.
model: The symbol uses four square shapes with different colors. Repetition and regular spacing connect them as a group. I would test whether the gaps remain clear at a small size.

title: Amazon: the arrow as a visual clue
script: Look beneath the Amazon wordmark. The orange curved arrow starts under the letter A and points toward the letter Z. Those are visible details we can point to. Its curved shape may also look like a smile to a viewer. That is a reading of the shape, not proof of how everyone will respond. In a client explanation, separate what you can see from the meaning you suggest. Then ask whether the detail still reads clearly when the wordmark is small or shown in one color.

gist.question: What distinction does the speaker make?
choices: A fixed meaning for every orange shape.
A recommendation to replace the arrow with a straight line.

details.question: Which letters does the speaker identify?
Which description is an interpretation?
choices: The arrow may resemble a smile.
The arrow is beneath the wordmark.
The arrow has an orange color.

phrases: Qualifies a resemblance rather than guaranteeing it.
response: Point to the arrow, describe its direction, and qualify one possible reading.
model: I can see an orange curved arrow beneath the wordmark, pointing from A toward Z. It may resemble a smile. I would check whether that detail remains clear at a small size and in one color.

title: McDonald’s: recognisable form with few details
script: The supplied McDonald's mark uses two joined arches that make an M-like shape. The color is yellow, and there is very little extra detail inside the mark. We can discuss shape and color as elements, and simplicity as a principle. Familiarity may help us recognise this particular mark, so recognition alone does not prove that any similar yellow shape would work for a new business. A designer still needs to check distinctiveness, clarity, and whether the mark fits the client's actual audience.

details.question: What basic shape does the speaker describe?
choices: Two joined arches forming an M-like mark.
Two separate circles forming a wordmark.
Four colored squares forming a grid.

details.question: Why is familiarity mentioned?
choices: Knowing the brand already can help recognition.
Familiarity proves the mark works for every new audience.
Familiarity removes the need for small-size testing.

phrases: Few internal features to distract from the main shape.
response: Describe the mark and explain why a new client’s logo needs its own audience test.
model: I notice two joined arches and a yellow color. The simple shape has few internal details, but familiarity also helps me recognise it. A new mark still needs its own clarity and audience test.
